name: a4
responses: Coalition action should generally prevail because it provides greater legitimacy, shares risks and costs, improves intelligence and operational capacity, and reduces the chance of escalation or diplomatic isolation. Acting alone may be faster, but speed can produce miscalculation, weaken international support, and make it harder to sustain the response. Exceptions may exist for imminent threats requiring immediate action, but as a default policy, building and acting through a coalition is safer and more durable.

A coalition should generally prevail because coordinated action provides greater legitimacy, shared intelligence and capabilities, burden-sharing, and stronger long-term political support. Acting alone may be faster initially, but it can create diplomatic isolation, reduce cooperation, and make the response harder to sustain. In situations requiring immediate action, a state may need to act first while rapidly bringing partners in—but the policy preference should remain coalition-based action.
